why_how.text: Nevada sets tougher penalties for young drivers, and knowing them before you start driving can protect your license for years.
A young driver who breaks an alcohol rule faces penalties even below the adult limit.

scenario.text: A seventeen-year-old driver is stopped and a breath test shows an alcohol level of three hundredths of one percent.

reasoning.text: For a young driver, a reading of at least two hundredths but under eight hundredths of one percent allows a revocation.

result.text: The driver can lose the license for one hundred eighty-five days, even though the reading is below the adult limit.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a young driver is safe from penalties as long as the alcohol reading is under the adult limit.

correction.text: A young driver's license can be revoked for one hundred eighty-five days at a reading as low as two hundredths of one percent.

memory_support.text: Low reading, long revocation; real DUI, adult rules.

prompt.text: A sixteen-year-old is convicted of a first DUI. Which penalties apply?

answer.text: The same penalties as a driver over twenty-one.

rationale.text: A young first-time DUI offender is treated like an adult offender, while a low reading alone brings the one hundred eighty-five-day revocation.

narration.text: This lesson covers the special rules for young drivers in Nevada. An applicant under eighteen for a license, a Driver Authorization Card or an instruction permit needs a parent or guardian to co-sign, and must sign an affidavit acknowledging the penalties that apply to young drivers. Those penalties are the heart of this lesson. We will look at what happens after a low alcohol reading or a court finding of impaired driving, which offenses can suspend or delay a license, and what happens when a young driver commits a first DUI offense. These rules apply long before most drivers expect them.

lines.text: Low reading: revoked one hundred eighty-five days.
Court finding of impaired driving: same revocation.

narration.text: Young drivers face an alcohol rule far stricter than the adult limit. A young driver's license can be revoked for one hundred eighty-five days when a blood, breath or urine test shows an alcohol level of at least two hundredths of one percent but less than eight hundredths of one percent by weight. Any court finding that a young driver drove under the influence of alcohol or a controlled substance also brings a one hundred eighty-five-day revocation. So the trigger can be either a test result or a court finding, and both lead to the same long revocation.

lines.text: Graffiti, drugs, alcohol: up to two years.
Firearm: up to one year, then two.

narration.text: Some penalties have nothing to do with driving. Graffiti or defacing property, crimes tied to alcohol or a controlled substance, any use or sale of a controlled substance, or buying, drinking or possessing alcohol can each mean suspension or delayed issuance for up to two years. Handling a firearm against state law means up to one year, and two years for a second offense. A first habitual-truancy offense brings thirty days to six months or a thirty-day delay, with longer terms for repeats. Joining a speed contest or trick driving display brings six months to two years.

title.text: Under the limit is not safe

lines.text: Adult limit does not protect teens.
Low reading still costs the license.
A first DUI means adult penalties.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many young drivers assume that staying under the adult alcohol limit keeps them safe. It does not. For a young driver, a reading of at least two hundredths of one percent is enough for a one hundred eighty-five-day revocation. And if the case becomes a first DUI offense, the young driver faces the same penalties as a driver over twenty-one, with no lighter juvenile version. So there are two separate outcomes to keep apart: the low-reading revocation, and the full adult penalties for a DUI. Neither one is a warning or a free pass.

Here is a quick check: a sixteen-year-old driver is convicted of a first DUI offense. Which penalties apply? Think it through before reading on. The young driver faces the same penalties as a driver over twenty-one. Nevada does not soften a first DUI because the driver is young. Compare that with a low alcohol reading that never becomes a DUI case: that reading alone brings a one hundred eighty-five-day revocation. Both outcomes are serious, but the DUI conviction places the young driver under the full set of adult penalties, the same ones any older offender faces.

lines.text: Many offenses can delay a license.

narration.text: To sum up, an applicant under eighteen needs a co-signing parent or guardian and must sign an affidavit about the young-driver penalties. A low alcohol reading or a court finding of impaired driving brings a one hundred eighty-five-day revocation, and a first DUI offense brings adult penalties. Graffiti, drug and alcohol offenses can suspend or delay a license for up to two years, a firearm offense for up to one year and then two, truancy for weeks to a year, and street racing or trick driving for six months to two years. Next we look at school attendance and driver education.

why_how.text: Permit and license applications for teens depend on school paperwork and practice records, so missing a form delays the whole process.
The number of practice hours depends on how far you live from an approved school.

scenario.text: Tara lives ten miles from an approved driver's education school and wants her license.

reasoning.text: Teens within thirty miles of an approved school complete fifty hours of supervised driving, ten of them at night.

result.text: Tara takes the standard path: driver's education plus fifty supervised hours with ten at night, recorded on the DMV form.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking any teen can skip driver's education by logging one hundred hours of practice.

correction.text: Only a teen more than thirty miles from an approved school who cannot take an online class may use the one-hundred-hour path.

memory_support.text: Fifty near the school, one hundred far away.

prompt.text: Ben lives fifty miles from any approved school and has no way to take an online class. How many practice hours does he log instead of driver's education?

answer.text: One hundred hours, ten of them in the dark.

rationale.text: Teens beyond thirty miles who cannot take an online class may log one hundred hours of behind-the-wheel driving, ten in the dark.

narration.text: This lesson covers the school and training paperwork a Nevada teen needs. Before an instruction permit, a student under eighteen proves school attendance. Before a license or Driver Authorization Card, a teen shows a driver's education certificate and a practice log. The number of practice hours depends on where the teen lives, and a clean record matters too. We will go through each form, the two paths for practice hours, the rule for students who were once declared habitual truants, and the six months without problems that must come before a license is issued.

lines.text: Permit applicants need a signed attendance form.
Graduates add a diploma or equivalency copy.
Former truants bring a new form.

narration.text: Anyone under eighteen applying for an instruction permit must give the DMV a Certification of Attendance signed by the principal or a designated school official confirming minimum attendance. A minor who has finished school submits the same form with a copy of a high school diploma or an equivalency such as a GED, HiSET or TASC, and the form must be signed and dated within the previous sixty days. A student once declared a habitual truant whose license or permit was suspended must bring a new attendance form showing current attendance before driving privileges are reinstated.

lines.text: Beginning Driver Experience Log in ink.
Schools can be local or online.

narration.text: A teen applying for a license or DAC must present a driver's education Certificate of Completion and the Beginning Driver Experience Log, filled in with blue or black ink before arriving for the drive test. Driver's education can be completed at a local DMV-approved school or online through a DMV-approved school. So most teens have two ways to take the course, in a classroom nearby or online, and either way the course must come from an approved school. The log is not something to fill in at the counter; it must be complete when you arrive.

lines.text: Within thirty miles: fifty hours, ten at night.
Beyond thirty, no online class: one hundred hours.
Motorcycle remote hours are daylight only.

narration.text: Teens within thirty miles of an approved driver's education school must complete fifty hours of supervised driving, ten of them at night, recorded on the official DMV form. Only a teen living more than thirty miles from an approved school who cannot take an online class may instead log one hundred hours of behind-the-wheel driving, ten of them in the dark. That remote path replaces the course, so it asks for twice the practice. For a motorcycle license on the remote path, all one hundred practice hours must be driven in daylight only, with no night riding counted.

lines.text: No online option is also required.

narration.text: Here is a trap. The one-hundred-hour path sounds like an easy way around driver's education, but it is narrow. A teen must live more than thirty miles from an approved school and also be unable to take an online class. If either condition is missing, the teen takes the course and logs the standard fifty supervised hours with ten at night. Another trap is the night requirement: both paths include ten hours after dark for cars. When a question mentions distance, check the online option as well before choosing the remote path and its larger number of hours.

Here is a quick check: Ben lives fifty miles from any approved driver's education school, and he has no way to take an online class. How many practice hours does he log instead of taking driver's education? Recall both conditions first. He qualifies for the remote path, so he logs one hundred hours of behind-the-wheel driving, ten of them in the dark. If Ben could take an online class, or lived within thirty miles of a school, he would take the course instead and log the standard fifty supervised hours, with ten of those at night.

lines.text: Six months without an at-fault crash.

narration.text: One more requirement completes this part. A minor must go six months without an at-fault crash, a moving violation conviction or any alcohol or drug conviction before receiving a license. So the paperwork is only half of the picture; the teen's driving record during the permit period matters too. To review: permit applicants bring a signed attendance form, graduates add a diploma copy dated within sixty days, license applicants bring the course certificate and the completed log, and practice hours follow the fifty-hour or one-hundred-hour path depending on distance and online access.

why_how.text: The permit is where most teens start, and its supervision rules decide who can ride along while you learn.
New teen drivers face passenger and curfew limits that apply even after the license is issued.

scenario.text: Jake, a new driver who just turned seventeen, wants to drive two classmates home from practice at eleven at night.

reasoning.text: For six months he may not carry non-family passengers under eighteen, and minors may not drive between ten at night and five in the morning except to or from a scheduled event.

result.text: Driving home from a scheduled practice may fit the curfew exception, but the classmates still cannot ride with him during his first six months.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the curfew ends once a teen has held a license for six months.

correction.text: The curfew lasts until the driver turns eighteen, no matter when the license was issued.

memory_support.text: Six months to hold, six months family-only, home by ten.

prompt.text: Who may sit beside a Class C permit holder as the supervising driver?

answer.text: A licensed driver twenty-one or older with at least one year of licensed experience.

rationale.text: A Class C permit holder may drive only with a licensed driver who is twenty-one or older, has at least a year of experience and sits beside them.

narration.text: This lesson covers the instruction permit and the limits on new teen drivers. You will see what it takes to get a permit, how long it lasts, who must sit beside you while you practice, and how motorcycle and moped permits differ. Then we turn to the rules that follow teens after they earn a license: how long the permit must be held first, the passenger limit during the first months, and the nighttime curfew. Several of these rules involve six months, so we will finish by lining them up so you can tell them apart. Each rule is short.

lines.text: Be at least fifteen and a half.

narration.text: To get a permit you must be at least fifteen and a half, complete an application, pass a vision test and a knowledge test on traffic laws, signs, markings and safe driving, and have a parent or guardian available to authorize it. A Nevada instruction permit is valid for one year and must be carried whenever the holder drives. A Class C permit holder may drive only with a licensed driver who is twenty-one or older, has at least one year of licensed experience, and sits in the seat beside the permit holder. Anyone else in that seat does not meet the rule.

lines.text: Supervisor rides a motorcycle in sight.

narration.text: Motorcycle and moped permits work differently. A Class C supervisor sits in the seat beside you, but a motorcycle or moped permit supervisor must ride a motorcycle within direct sight of the permit holder and may not be in a car or truck. A Class M or M-Z permit holder rides in daylight only, carries no passengers, and stays off limited-access highways and freeways. So the motorcycle learner rides alone on the bike, during the day, on ordinary roads, with a supervisor close by on another motorcycle rather than in a following vehicle.

lines.text: Hold the permit at least six months.
Family-only young passengers for six months.
No driving ten at night to five.

narration.text: Applicants under eighteen must hold an instruction permit for at least six months before applying for a license. For their first six months of driving, new licensees who were sixteen or seventeen at issuance may not carry passengers under eighteen except immediate family members. A minor also may not drive between ten at night and five in the morning unless driving to or from a scheduled event, and this curfew lasts until the driver turns eighteen, regardless of when the license was issued. So a teen licensed at seventeen and a half still keeps the curfew until the eighteenth birthday.

Here is the trap: three different rules all use six months. First, a teen must hold the instruction permit for at least six months before applying for a license. Second, for the first six months of licensed driving, no non-family passengers under eighteen may ride along. Third, a minor must stay free of at-fault crashes and moving, alcohol or drug convictions for six months before licensing. When a question mentions six months, ask which stage it is about: before the license, the clean-record period, or after the license, the passenger limit. The curfew is different again and lasts until eighteen.

Here is a quick check: you hold a Class C instruction permit and want to practice in the family car. Who may sit beside you as the supervising driver? Recall the three conditions before reading on. The supervisor must be a licensed driver who is twenty-one or older, has at least one year of licensed experience, and sits in the seat beside you. A nineteen-year-old licensed sibling does not qualify, and neither does an experienced adult sitting in the back seat. For a motorcycle permit the rule changes: the supervisor rides another motorcycle within direct sight.

lines.text: Permit at fifteen and a half, valid a year.

narration.text: Let us review. A permit requires age fifteen and a half, an application, vision and knowledge tests and a parent or guardian's authorization, and it is valid for one year and carried whenever you drive. A Class C supervisor is twenty-one or older with a year of experience and sits beside you, while motorcycle supervisors ride within sight. Teens hold the permit six months, carry only family passengers under eighteen for six months, and observe the ten-at-night to five-in-the-morning curfew until eighteen. Next we look at license classes, codes and endorsements.

why_how.text: Each license class covers certain vehicles, so knowing your class tells you what you may drive and tow.
Restriction codes and endorsements on your card change what you are allowed to do behind the wheel.

scenario.text: Rosa holds a Class C license and wants to tow a travel trailer rated well above ten thousand pounds.

reasoning.text: Class C may tow ten thousand pounds or less; the J endorsement allows heavier towing within seventy feet and the stated combined weight.

result.text: Rosa needs the J endorsement, and if the combination ever topped the combined limit, a Class A license would be required.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a Class C license lets you tow any trailer as long as it fits on the hitch.

correction.text: Class C towing stops at ten thousand pounds; heavier towing needs the J endorsement, and the heaviest combinations need Class A.

memory_support.text: C for cars, J for heavier towing, A for the biggest.

prompt.text: A license shows restriction code G. What does it mean?

rationale.text: Among the common restriction codes, G means daylight driving only, while B means glasses or contacts and F means added rearview mirrors.

narration.text: This lesson explains what different licenses allow. Every license class requires vision and knowledge tests, and a road test in the type of vehicle to be driven may also be required. We will look at what the Class C license covers and may tow, how the other classes compare, what the common restriction codes mean, and what endorsements add. We will finish with the motorcycle path, including permits, safety courses and the requirements for a motorcycle license. By the end you should be able to read a license and know which vehicles its holder may drive.

lines.text: Tow ten thousand pounds or less.

narration.text: Class C covers cars, vans and pickups. A Class C driver may tow a vehicle of ten thousand pounds or less, and any combination of vehicles may not exceed seventy feet. Any Nevada license class lets you ride a moped, or you can apply for a Class M license restricted to mopeds only. A Class C holder who also wants to ride a motorcycle must pass a written test on motorcycle laws and practices and a motorcycle drive test. So Class C is the everyday license, with a clear towing ceiling and a separate path for motorcycles.

Class A covers combinations rated over twenty-six thousand pounds with a trailer over ten thousand pounds. Class B covers a single vehicle rated over twenty-six thousand pounds that may tow less than ten thousand pounds. Class M covers motorcycles and mopeds. A commercial motor vehicle is one used in commerce with a heavy weight rating, or designed for sixteen or more people including the driver, or carrying hazardous materials. Commercial drivers must pass additional knowledge and skills tests described in the separate Commercial Driver's License Handbook, which this course does not cover.

lines.text: An endorsement adds a skill-based privilege.
J: heavier towing for Class C.
F: commercial exemption for some drivers.

narration.text: An endorsement allows driving a vehicle that needs more skill than a typical vehicle, and each one needs additional tests. The J endorsement lets a Class C driver tow a vehicle or combination rated above ten thousand pounds, as long as the combination stays within seventy feet and twenty-six thousand pounds; above that, a Class A license is required. The F endorsement is a commercial-license exemption for firefighters with fire equipment, military members driving military vehicles on active duty, and certain farm employees or family hauling supplies near the farm.

A motorcycle permit issued between fifteen and a half and eighteen lasts one year, but one issued after age seventeen expires on the eighteenth birthday; at eighteen or older it lasts six months and can be renewed only once every five years. Passing an approved motorcycle safety course may replace the motorcycle tests, but failing the DMV motorcycle skills test two or more times permanently bars future motorcycle permits. A motorcycle license requires age sixteen, a vision test, the general and motorcycle knowledge tests and the skills test, and riders must wear a helmet.

lines.text: Class C: up to ten thousand pounds.

narration.text: Here is a trap about towing. A Class C license sounds like it covers anything a pickup can pull, but its towing limit is ten thousand pounds, and the whole combination may not exceed seventy feet. Towing more than ten thousand pounds needs the J endorsement, which still caps the combination at seventy feet and twenty-six thousand pounds. Above that combined weight, a Class A license is required. So read the weight first. Up to ten thousand is ordinary Class C, the middle range needs the J endorsement, and the heaviest combinations belong to Class A.

Here is a quick check: a driver's license shows restriction code G. What does that code mean? Recall the list of common codes before reading on. Code G means daylight driving only. It is easy to mix up with the others: B means glasses or contacts, F means added rearview mirrors, and the numbers six, seven and eight call for a yearly vision exam, a yearly medical letter and a yearly driving test. JN marks an instruction permit. Because restrictions narrow what a license allows, a driver with code G may not drive after dark.

lines.text: Every class: vision and knowledge tests.

narration.text: To review, every license class requires vision and knowledge tests, and a road test in the vehicle type may also be required. Class C covers cars, vans and pickups and tows up to ten thousand pounds, Class A covers heavy combinations, Class B heavy single vehicles, and Class M motorcycles and mopeds. Restriction codes such as B, F and G narrow what a license allows, while endorsements such as J add a privilege after extra tests. Any class may ride a moped, but a motorcycle needs written and riding tests, a helmet, and a skills test you may not fail twice. Next we look at renewals and changes.

why_how.text: Renewing on time and reporting changes keeps your license valid and your records accurate.

scenario.text: Omar moves across town and plans to update his address when his license comes up for renewal in three years.

reasoning.text: Nevada law requires reporting any change of address or name to the DMV within thirty days.

result.text: Omar must report the move within thirty days, which he can do online, at an office or by mail.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the DMV's mailed renewal notice makes renewal the DMV's responsibility.

correction.text: Renewing on or before the expiration date is the driver's responsibility, even though a notice is mailed.

memory_support.text: Move or rename? Thirty days to tell the DMV.

prompt.text: Lena gets married and takes a new last name. How must she update her license?

answer.text: In person, with legal proof of the new name, within thirty days.

rationale.text: Name changes are always made in person with legal proof, and every change of name or address must be reported within thirty days.

narration.text: This lesson covers what happens after you hold a license. You will learn who is responsible for renewing, what renewal may involve, how active-duty members renew from out of state, how quickly changes of address or name must be reported and how to make them, what to do if a license is lost or damaged, and who may receive a restricted license. These are the everyday rules that keep a license valid. Missing a renewal date or a reporting deadline is an easy way to end up driving with a license that is no longer in order.

The expiration date is printed on the front of the license, and renewing on or before it is the driver's responsibility, even though a renewal notice is mailed. Renewal may call for vision, knowledge and on-road driving tests to re-evaluate the driver and decide on restrictions. Nevada does not automatically extend licenses for military personnel, but active-duty members temporarily out of state may renew by mail. If a license is lost, stolen or becomes illegible, it should be replaced immediately with a duplicate, online or in person, using the record and photo on file.

lines.text: Report address or name within thirty days.

narration.text: Nevada law requires you to report any change of address or name to the DMV within thirty days. Addresses can be changed online, at a DMV office, or by mail with the change-of-address form, but commercial license holders must do it in person. Name changes are always made in person with legal proof of the new name. So the method depends on what changed: an address has several routes, while a name has only one. Either way, the thirty-day deadline is the same, and waiting until your next renewal does not meet it. Plan the change early.

lines.text: A restricted license is an exception.
Fourteen or fifteen with hardship or school need.

narration.text: Here is a trap. A restricted license can sound like an early permit for anyone young, but it is a special-circumstance exception. Restricted licenses may go to drivers aged fourteen and fifteen who show family hardship or need to drive to and from school, and to people who have served half of a suspension or revocation. Without one of those circumstances, a young driver follows the ordinary permit path, starting at fifteen and a half. So when a question describes a fourteen-year-old, look for a hardship or school-travel reason before deciding that a restricted license is possible.

lines.text: Lena takes a new last name.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Lena gets married and takes a new last name. How must she update her Nevada license, and how soon? Think about both parts before reading on. She must make the change in person, with legal proof of the new name, because name changes are always made in person. And she must report it within thirty days, the same deadline that applies to any change of name or address. If she had only moved, she could have changed the address online, at an office or by mail, but a name change has no online route. Both parts matter.

To review, the expiration date is on the front of your license, and renewing on time is your responsibility even with a mailed notice. Renewal may include vision, knowledge and road tests, and active-duty members out of state may renew by mail. Changes of address or name must be reported within thirty days: addresses online, at an office or by mail, names only in person with proof. Replace a lost, stolen or illegible license right away with a duplicate. Restricted licenses are exceptions for hardship, school travel or a half-served suspension. Next we turn to ID cards and fees.

why_how.text: A Nevada ID card has its own rules, and getting one can affect your driving privilege.
Fees are set by state law, so knowing which fee applies helps you plan a visit or a reinstatement.

scenario.text: Grace, who holds a Nevada license, applies for a Nevada ID card instead.

reasoning.text: Being issued an ID card automatically surrenders your driving privilege and any other ID card, whether or not you have it with you.

result.text: Grace gives up her driving privilege when the ID card is issued, so she should apply only if she means to stop driving.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking you can hold both a Nevada ID card and a driving privilege at once.

correction.text: Issuing an ID card automatically surrenders the driving privilege, except for seasonal resident ID applicants.

memory_support.text: ID card in, driving privilege out.

prompt.text: How long does a standard Nevada ID card last, and when does it expire?

answer.text: Eight years, on the holder's birthday.

rationale.text: A Nevada ID card requires age ten or older and lasts eight years, expiring on the birthday unless limited-term immigration documents were used.

narration.text: This lesson covers Nevada ID cards, the optional designations you can add to a license or ID, and the fees the handbook lists. You will see who can get an ID card, how long it lasts, what getting one surrenders, and how traffic citations follow an ID card holder. Then we look at the veteran designation, the medical indicator and organ donation, a short public-safety note on recognizing sex trafficking, and finally the license, permit, change and reinstatement fees. Fees are set by Nevada state law and can change, so treat the amounts as the handbook's current figures.

lines.text: Age ten or older; eight years.

narration.text: A Nevada ID card requires age ten or older and lasts eight years, expiring on the birthday. If limited-term immigration documents were used, the card expires on the departure date, or one year after issuance when no date is listed. Being issued an ID card automatically surrenders your driving privilege and any ID card from Nevada or another state, whether or not you have it with you; seasonal resident ID applicants are the exception. Traffic citations issued to an ID card holder count against future driving privileges, and twelve or more demerits in twelve months means reinstatement first.

lines.text: Medical indicator with a physician report.
Organ Donor at issuance or renewal.

narration.text: Several designations can be added to a card. An honorably discharged veteran can add a veteran designation by bringing proof of honorable discharge and signing a release to the Nevada Department of Veterans Services. An optional medical indicator, a medical symbol on the front of the card, needs a completed Confidential Physician Report naming one listed medical code. Organ Donor can be added at original issuance, renewal or an address change, and a minor's parent or guardian signs an affidavit accepting that they cannot amend or revoke the donation. Donations to related funds can also be made through the DMV.

The handbook also includes a public-safety note on sex trafficking. Possible signs include a person not knowing where they are, not holding their own ID or passport, having their communication controlled by someone else, and acting fearful or submissive. If you notice these signs, the handbook is clear that a suspected trafficker should never be confronted. The point for a driver is awareness: people on the road, at rest stops or in parking lots may show these signs, and the safe response is to notice them without putting yourself or the possible victim at risk by confronting anyone.

lines.text: Set by state law; they can change.
Lower fees at sixty-five and older.

narration.text: Fees are set by Nevada state law and can change. Under age sixty-five, an original license costs forty-one dollars and twenty-five cents, and an instruction permit costs twenty-two dollars and twenty-five cents. Drivers sixty-five and older pay seventeen dollars and twenty-five cents for an original, duplicate, renewal or instruction permit, and ID cards for ages ten to seventeen cost nine dollars and twenty-five cents. A change of address alone costs three dollars and twenty-five cents, and each knowledge and skills retest costs ten dollars after the twenty-five dollar initial test fee.

lines.text: Alcohol offense: higher fee plus victim's fee.

narration.text: Reinstatement fees depend on the reason the license was lost. Reinstatement after an alcohol or controlled-substance offense costs one hundred twenty dollars plus a thirty-five dollar victim's fee, while reinstatement for any other offense costs seventy-five dollars. Any suspension, revocation or cancellation also requires paying the original-license fee and any testing fees that apply, on top of the reinstatement fee. Reinstating a commercial license also requires paying a non-commercial reinstatement fee. So losing a license costs more than the reinstatement fee alone; several fees stack together before you can drive again.

Here is a quick check: how long does a standard Nevada ID card last, and when does it expire? Recall the age rule and the term before reading on. A Nevada ID card requires age ten or older and lasts eight years, expiring on the holder's birthday. The exception is a card based on limited-term immigration documents: that card expires on the departure date, or one year after issuance if no date is listed. So the standard ID card and the limited-term ID card can end years apart, and the documents used decide which rule applies.

lines.text: ID cards: age ten, eight years.
Fees are set by state law.

narration.text: Let us sum up. A Nevada ID card requires age ten or older and lasts eight years, or ends at the departure date or after one year when limited-term documents were used. Being issued one surrenders your driving privilege, and citations still count against future privileges. Veteran, medical and organ donor designations each have their own proof or form. Fees are set by state law: drivers sixty-five and older and young ID card applicants pay less, and reinstatement after an alcohol offense costs more than after other offenses, with the original-license and testing fees added on top. That completes the licensing chapter.
